gaps.title: Per-class accuracy impact of augmentation on Fashion-MNIST garments

impact.why: Explains the mechanism behind aggregate accuracy changes and provides actionable guidance about which garment classes benefit from each augmentation type.

novelty.why: None of the prior works examine per-class accuracy deltas from basic image augmentation specifically on Fashion-MNIST, nor do they analyze how horizontal-flip augmentation differentially affects morphologically similar or asymmetric garment classes (e.g., shirt vs. T-shirt/top). The closest works address class-wise augmentation effects in other domains (batik motifs, liver lesions) but not this specific dataset or hypothesis about flip-induced label ambiguity.

feasibility.why: Analysis is derived entirely from models already trained in the core experiment, requiring only CPU-based inference and plotting with no additional GPU runs.

testability.why: Per-class accuracy delta is directly measurable from stored predictions, though with 2 seeds significance assessment is limited to exploratory framing.

gaps.approach: Extract per-class precision, recall, F1, and full confusion matrices from augmented and non-augmented trained models across seeds 42 and 123 (four models total). Compute Δaccuracy and Δconfusion-cell for each of the 10 classes and each of the 100 class pairs, then visualize as a per-class accuracy delta bar chart and annotated delta confusion matrix; all analysis runs on CPU using stored model predictions from the core experiment's GPU runs.
gaps.question: Does basic image augmentation disproportionately improve or reduce accuracy on specific Fashion-MNIST garment classes, particularly for morphologically similar or asymmetric classes?
gaps.why_open: (Yee 2026) notes that morphologically distinctive categories such as trousers, bags, and footwear show high discriminative performance but does not study how augmentation changes per-class accuracy. All papers reporting augmentation effects on Fashion-MNIST (Greeshma et al. 2019; Mukhamediev 2024; Hassan et al. 2025; Kayed et al. 2020) aggregate accuracy into a single number, obscuring which garment classes drive gains or losses. (Agarwal et al. 2025) found that augmentation did not consistently improve accuracy for the best-performing model on CIFAR-10, suggesting class-level heterogeneity, but no analogous per-class study exists for Fashion-MNIST. Fashion-MNIST has known confusable class pairs such as T-shirt versus shirt versus pullover where flip-induced distortions might introduce label-ambiguous training examples and hurt recognition.
gaps.hypothesis: Augmentation will disproportionately help symmetric garment classes (trousers, pullovers, coats) for which horizontal flips are valid invariances, while potentially reducing accuracy for fine-grained confusable classes such as shirt versus T-shirt/top where flipped images introduce label ambiguity.
gaps.data_needed: Fashion-MNIST test set (10,000 images, 10 balanced classes); predictions from the four trained models produced in the core experiment.

gaps.title: Individual augmentation type ablation on Fashion-MNIST CNN

impact.why: Directly answers a practitioner question about which cheap augmentation to prioritize and fills an explicitly identified open problem in the brief.

novelty.why: The prior work applies augmentation broadly to improve Fashion-MNIST accuracy but none isolates and compares the individual contributions of horizontal flip, translation, and rotation via ablation or Shapley-style decomposition on a small CNN; the closest papers (e.g., 'State-of-the-Art Results' and 'Optimized Neural Networks') use augmentation as a bundle without disaggregating per-type effects.

feasibility.why: 14 short GPU runs using infrastructure identical to the core experiment are completable in one Colab session with minimal code changes.

testability.why: Test accuracy per condition provides a clear, quantitative outcome that unambiguously distinguishes each augmentation type's contribution.

gaps.approach: Train the identical small CNN under seven augmentation conditions: no augmentation, flip-only, translate-only, rotate-only, flip+translate, flip+rotate, and all-three combined; use seeds 42 and 123 for each, yielding 14 GPU runs of 5 epochs each on Fashion-MNIST. Compute per-condition test accuracy and a Shapley-style additive decomposition of accuracy gains attributable to each augmentation type. Produce a bar chart of accuracy by condition and a delta table relative to the no-augmentation baseline.
gaps.question: Which individual augmentation type — horizontal flip, random translation, or random rotation — contributes most to small-CNN test accuracy gains on Fashion-MNIST?
gaps.why_open: Surveys of augmentation (Shorten et al. 2019) and (Zeng 2024) catalog many techniques but provide no ablation isolating each geometric transform's individual contribution for small CNNs on Fashion-MNIST. (Hnatushenko et al. 2023) found that single augmentation types did not yield significant improvements for satellite imagery while combinations helped, but this finding has not been replicated on Fashion-MNIST. (Kurban et al. 2026) performs architecture-specific augmentation grid searches on CIFAR-10 but not on Fashion-MNIST, leaving unclear which transform drives any accuracy gains in the core experiment. The open problems section explicitly identifies isolating individual augmentation contributions as an unresolved question in the field.
gaps.hypothesis: Horizontal flip augmentation will contribute the largest individual accuracy gain because Fashion-MNIST garment classes have strong left-right symmetry invariance, making flipped images valid additional training examples, whereas small rotations and translations provide weaker or noisier signal for symmetric garment classes.
gaps.data_needed: Fashion-MNIST via torchvision (60,000 train / 10,000 test); no additional data required.

gaps.title: Augmentation magnitude sensitivity grid search on Fashion-MNIST

impact.why: Provides practical, dataset-specific augmentation guidance absent from all surveyed papers and validates or challenges the core experiment's unjustified default magnitudes.

novelty.why: Targeted searches returned no related papers.

feasibility.why: 40 GPU runs are feasible on Colab but require session management and approximately 3.5 total GPU hours, introducing scheduling overhead.

testability.why: The 5×4 accuracy matrix yields a clear 2D landscape with an identifiable optimum and direct comparison against the no-augmentation baseline.

gaps.approach: Perform a 5×4 grid search over rotation magnitudes {0°, 5°, 10°, 20°, 30°} × translation ranges {0%, 5%, 10%, 20%} with all conditions including horizontal flip; train each combination with seeds 42 and 123 for 5 epochs on Fashion-MNIST, yielding 40 GPU runs. Report accuracy as a 2D heat map, fit a quadratic response surface to identify the empirical optimum, and note where the core experiment's defaults fall relative to that optimum.
gaps.question: How sensitive is small-CNN generalization on Fashion-MNIST to the specific magnitude of rotation angle and translation range used during training?
gaps.why_open: (Kurban et al. 2026) provides systematic augmentation hyperparameter grid search for CNN architectures on CIFAR-10 but not on Fashion-MNIST. (Lopes et al. 2021) introduces the Affinity/Diversity framework predicting a tradeoff at excessive augmentation magnitudes, but does not empirically validate it for Fashion-MNIST with small CNNs. The core experiment fixes rotation at ≤10° and translation at ≤10% without empirical justification, and (Greeshma et al. 2019) uses cropping, rotation, and flipping without reporting which magnitudes were tested. No paper in the corpus performs a controlled search over rotation and translation magnitudes for a small CNN on Fashion-MNIST, leaving optimal augmentation parameters unknown for this dataset.
gaps.hypothesis: There is an inverted-U relationship between augmentation magnitude and test accuracy, with peak accuracy at moderate magnitudes around 10–15° rotation and 10–15% translation, and declining performance at larger magnitudes where augmented images no longer resemble realistic garment images.
gaps.data_needed: Fashion-MNIST via torchvision; no additional data required.

gaps.title: CNN depth scaling of augmentation benefit on Fashion-MNIST

impact.why: Directly addresses the explicitly stated open problem about augmentation scaling with model size with practical implications for architecture selection.

novelty.why: None of the prior works systematically compare augmentation benefit (Δaccuracy) as a function of CNN depth/parameter count on Fashion-MNIST; the closest work ('Building Efficient Lightweight CNN Models') uses augmentation with lightweight CNNs on Fashion-MNIST but does not isolate the interaction between model depth and augmentation gain as the primary research question.

feasibility.why: 12 GPU runs using existing training infrastructure require only architectural variations in one code file and fit in one Colab session.

testability.why: Augmentation benefit Δaccuracy per architecture is directly measurable, though with 2 seeds the confidence intervals will be wide.

gaps.approach: Construct three small CNN variants with increasing depth: 1-block (~20K parameters), 2-block (~80K parameters), and 3-block (~250K parameters), holding optimizer, learning rate, and batch size fixed. Train each with and without full augmentation using seeds 42 and 123 for 5 epochs on Fashion-MNIST (12 GPU runs total), then plot augmentation benefit Δaccuracy versus parameter count and report the interaction between model depth and augmentation condition.
gaps.question: Does the absolute accuracy gain from basic image augmentation on Fashion-MNIST differ systematically between 1-block, 2-block, and 3-block small CNNs?
gaps.why_open: (Mohammadagha et al. 2025) compares augmentation and dropout effects in a baseline CNN versus ResNet-18 on Imagenette but does not isolate the augmentation gain (Δaccuracy) as a function of model depth on Fashion-MNIST. (Hassan et al. 2025) achieves 98.30% with a deep ResCNN with augmentation but provides no no-augmentation baseline for the same architecture, preventing measurement of augmentation benefit. (Isong 2025) builds lightweight CNNs of different sizes on Fashion-MNIST but does not vary augmentation as a factor. The open problems section explicitly states that whether small CNNs benefit more or less from augmentation than larger architectures is unresolved.
gaps.hypothesis: The absolute accuracy gain from augmentation will be larger for shallower CNNs because capacity-limited models are more prone to underfitting the augmented distribution, leaving more room for the augmentation's implicit regularization to improve generalization.
gaps.data_needed: Fashion-MNIST via torchvision; no additional data required.

gaps.title: Training epoch horizon for augmentation benefit plateau on Fashion-MNIST

impact.why: Primarily a methodological contribution validating or challenging the 5-epoch assumption; useful but narrower than architectural or per-class findings.

novelty.why: No paper in the corpus plots augmentation benefit as a function of training epoch count specifically for small CNNs on Fashion-MNIST.

feasibility.why: Longer runs up to 50 epochs are straightforward to implement but require session management and checkpoint infrastructure to avoid data loss.

testability.why: The augmentation benefit curve against epoch count provides a clear, quantitative answer about the plateau point and asymptotic gain.

gaps.approach: Train the same small CNN with and without full augmentation for epoch counts {5, 15, 30, 50} using seeds 42 and 123 on Fashion-MNIST (16 GPU runs total). For each epoch count, compute the augmentation benefit Δtest accuracy and plot a benefit-versus-epochs curve; fit a saturation curve to estimate the plateau epoch and extrapolate the asymptotic benefit.
gaps.question: At what number of training epochs does the test accuracy benefit of basic image augmentation plateau when training a small CNN on Fashion-MNIST?
gaps.why_open: The open problems section explicitly flags whether augmentation gains plateau quickly with more training epochs and whether 5 epochs is sufficient to observe the full effect as an unresolved question. (Thanapol et al. 2020) studies augmentation injection timing on CIFAR-10 at epoch 30 but does not measure the benefit growth curve as a function of total epochs. (Kurban et al. 2026) trains architectures to a fixed epoch count without studying the augmentation benefit trajectory over time. No paper in the corpus reports an accuracy-gap-versus-epochs curve for simple augmentations on Fashion-MNIST, making the 5-epoch assumption in the core experiment potentially premature.
gaps.hypothesis: Augmentation benefit will grow monotonically for at least 20–30 epochs and will not have plateaued at 5 epochs, meaning the core experiment underestimates the full accuracy gain that augmentation would deliver with longer training.
gaps.data_needed: Fashion-MNIST via torchvision; no additional data required.
gaps.compute_needed: 16 GPU runs with varying epoch counts; 50-epoch runs take approximately 20–25 min each on Colab T4, totaling roughly 3 hours; feasible with session management and checkpoint saving.

gaps.title: Optimizer-augmentation interaction for Fashion-MNIST small CNN

impact.why: A useful practical finding for practitioners choosing optimizers alongside augmentation, but narrower in scope than architectural depth or per-class insights.

novelty.why: The prior work compares Adam vs. SGD on various image classification tasks, but none isolates the interaction effect between optimizer choice and data augmentation on Fashion-MNIST, which is the core question here.

feasibility.why: 8 GPU runs in a 2×2 factorial fit easily in one Colab session using identical architecture and training code with only the optimizer parameter changed.

testability.why: The interaction effect is directly computable from four accuracy values, but confidence is limited by only 2 seeds per cell and short 5-epoch training.

gaps.approach: Run a 2×2 factorial experiment crossing {Adam, SGD with matched initial learning rate} × {no augmentation, full augmentation} with seeds 42 and 123 for 5 epochs on Fashion-MNIST, yielding 8 GPU runs total. Report test accuracy for each cell, compute the interaction effect as the difference in augmentation benefit between optimizers, and visualize as a 2×2 interaction plot with an effect size estimate rather than a formal significance test given only 2 seeds.
gaps.question: Does the accuracy benefit of basic image augmentation on Fashion-MNIST differ significantly depending on whether Adam or SGD is used as the optimizer?
gaps.why_open: (Sayın et al. 2025) systematically benchmarks 8 optimizers across Fashion-MNIST in CNNs but does not cross optimizer choice with augmentation as an independent variable. (Marin et al. 2020) compares Adam and SGD with regularization techniques on Fashion-MNIST but does not test augmentation as a separate factorial factor. (S et al. 2024) evaluates multiple optimizers on Fashion-MNIST without varying augmentation. The core experiment fixes the optimizer to isolate augmentation effects, but this means the measured augmentation benefit may be optimizer-specific, limiting the generalizability of its conclusions.
gaps.hypothesis: Adam will show a smaller augmentation benefit than SGD because Adam's adaptive per-parameter learning rates provide implicit regularization that partially overlaps with augmentation's anti-overfitting function, leaving less room for augmentation to further improve generalization under Adam.
gaps.data_needed: Fashion-MNIST via torchvision; no additional data required.
